identity.title: Data Shapley in One Training Run

problem.claim: Attribute the contribution of data to a particular model training run, including foundation-model pretraining.

gap.claim: Traditional Data Shapley requires retraining on many data subsets, making it computationally infeasible at scale and unsuitable for evaluating a specific training run.

contributions.claim: Introduces In-Run Data Shapley, which avoids model retraining by calculating Shapley values for each gradient-update iteration and accumulating them during training.
Presents techniques for scaling In-Run Data Shapley to foundation-model size.
Reports case studies examining pretraining-data contribution and implications for copyright in generative AI and data curation.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe In-Run Data Shapley as a new concept designed to assess data contribution for a particular model without retraining.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the most optimized implementation adds negligible runtime overhead relative to standard model training.
The authors report that the efficiency improvement enables data attribution during foundation-model pretraining.
The authors report fresh insights from case studies on pretraining-data contribution and discuss copyright and curation implications.

narrative_sequence.summary: Data Shapley provides a principled framework for attributing data contribution.
Retraining-based Data Shapley is costly at large scale and cannot assess a specific training run.
The paper introduces In-Run Data Shapley, accumulating per-iteration Shapley values without retraining.
The authors present scaling techniques and report negligible overhead in the most optimized implementation.
The method is applied through case studies of pretraining-data contribution, copyright, and data curation.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a practical limitation—retraining cost and inability to target one run—to an iteration-level attribution mechanism that accumulates values throughout training.

lessons.interpretation: A method can be framed more compellingly when its computational design directly addresses both scalability and the concrete evaluation target.
lessons.application: When introducing a new attribution method, explicitly map each operational limitation to a corresponding algorithmic mechanism and state the intended unit of analysis.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the proposed mechanism does not directly resolve the stated limitation or when the target use case is not a specific training run.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the scaling techniques, model sizes, datasets, runtime measurements, or quantitative case-study findings.
The basis and scope of the reported copyright and curation implications are not detailed.
The abstract does not provide comparisons beyond standard model training overhead.
